label: Annual CO₂ increase at Mauna Loa, 1959–2025
source: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, co2_gr_mlo.txt (https://gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends/, retrieved 2026-11-06); Lan, Tans & Thoning, NOAA/GML, with Keeling (Scripps) before 1974; NOAA data, freely available, citation requested
note: increase of the CO₂ mole fraction from January 1 to December 31, ppm per year (uncertainty about 0.11 ppm); rising, with large year-to-year swings from El Niño (1998, 2016, 2023–24) and the Pinatubo dip (1992)

label: Annual global methane increase, 1984–2025
source: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory, ch4_gr_gl.txt (https://gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends_ch4/, retrieved 2026-11-06); Lan, Thoning & Dlugokencky, NOAA/GML; Dlugokencky et al. (1994), J. Geophys. Res. 99:17021–17043; NOAA data, freely available, citation requested
note: increase of the globally averaged CH₄ mole fraction from January 1 to December 31, ppb per year (column sd: its uncertainty); falling from the 1980s, with spikes in 1991 and 1998, near zero 1999–2006, rising again since 2007 to a peak in 2020–21

label: Antarctic ozone minimum, annual means 1979–2025
source: NASA Ozone Watch, Annual Records, table of means (https://ozonewatch.gsfc.nasa.gov/statistics/annual_data.html, last updated 2025-10-20)
note: min_ozone: mean over 21 September–16 October of the daily minimum Southern Hemisphere total ozone (DU), the yearly means of NASA's daily series; hole_area: mean ozone hole area over 7 September–13 October (million km²); no data for 1995; year-to-year changes in the polar vortex are part of the noise

label: Arctic sea ice extent in September, 1979–2026
source: NSIDC Sea Ice Index, Version 4 (G02135), N_09_extent_v4.0.csv (https://nsidc.org/data/g02135, retrieved 2026-11-06); Fetterer, Knowles, Meier, Savoie & Windnagel, doi:10.7265/a98x-0f50; US government work (NOAA@NSIDC)
note: monthly mean extent of the September minimum, million km² (area: the ice-covered area); decline since the 1990s, the record low in 2012, and little net change since about 2007

label: Blood levels by age
source: NeuroImage paper
note: three age groups with top two age groups about the same; heteroskedastic

label: Central England temperature, annual means 1659–2025
source: Met Office Hadley Centre, HadCET v2.1 meantemp_monthly_totals.txt (https://www.metoffice.gov.uk/hadobs/hadcet/, retrieved 2026-11-06); Manley (1974), Q. J. R. Meteorol. Soc. 100:389–405; Parker, Legg & Folland (1992), Int. J. Climatol. 12:317–342; © Crown copyright, Met Office, Open Government Licence v3
note: annual mean temperature, °C, of a triangle between Lancashire, London and Bristol; monthly values before 1699 are given to the whole or half degree, so less precise; nearly level for two and a half centuries (cold 1690s), warmer since about 1990

label: Chess recall scores
source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4361603/
note: hump

label: Cleveland curve, three pieces
source: artificial example from W. S. Cleveland, Visualizing Data (Hobart Press, 1993); this draw by tools/make-cleveland-curve.mjs, seed 1993
note: three smooth pieces of 50 points each, f = 5 − √(1 − z), 5 + sin(2πz), 5 + z²/2 with z from 0 to 1 in each; y = f + N(0, 0.2²); column f is the noise-free curve; the first piece ends in a vertical tangent

label: Colorado River annual peak flow at Lees Ferry, water years 1921–2023
source: USGS National Water Information System, peak streamflow for site 09380000, Colorado River at Lees Ferry, AZ (https://nwis.waterdata.usgs.gov/nwis/peak?site_no=09380000, retrieved 2026-11-06); USGS data, public domain
note: largest instantaneous flow of each water year (October–September), cubic feet per second (date: its day); Glen Canyon Dam, 15 miles upstream, began storing water in 1963 (water year 1963: 19,200 cfs, after 85,000 in 1962), which cut the spring floods to releases from the dam: a step down; the high-flow releases (1983–86 spills, the 1996 and later experiments) are visible after it; the historic 1884 peak (210,000 cfs, its date unknown) is left out

label: Daily bike rentals by temperature, Washington DC, 2011–2012
source: Fanaee-T (2013), Bike Sharing [Dataset], UCI Machine Learning Repository, doi:10.24432/C5W894 (CC BY 4.0); Capital Bikeshare system data; Fanaee-T & Gama (2014), Prog. Artif. Intell. 2:113–127
note: rentals per day (casual and registered) against the day's temperature, °C (UCI's normalized temp × 41); rises with temperature and falls off on the hottest days; 2012 (yr = 1) has about 65% more rentals than 2011 at the same temperature, so the noise is two clusters, and days are serially correlated

label: Dog vs Human ages
source: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/829192v1.full
note: y ascending sharply then slowly or leveling; non-decreasing; data scraped from a figure in an early preprint of the paper (bioRxiv v1), so they may not match later versions

label: Fibers distance
source: https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2423437122
note: many duplicate x values; y ascending then level

label: Fuel economy by horsepower, cars of 1970–1982
source: Quinlan (1993), Auto MPG [Dataset], UCI Machine Learning Repository, doi:10.24432/C5859H (CC BY 4.0); from the StatLib library, Carnegie Mellon (1983 ASA Data Exposition)
note: 392 models (6 without horsepower dropped); miles per gallon falls steeply and then levels off with horsepower, and spreads more at low power; weight and model year explain much of the rest

label: Global surface temperature anomaly, 1880–2025
source: NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4), GLB.Ts+dSST.csv (https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/, retrieved 2026-11-06); GISTEMP Team (2026); Lenssen et al. (2019), J. Geophys. Res. Atmos. 124:6307–6326; NASA data, public domain
note: annual (January–December) mean land-ocean temperature anomaly, °C relative to 1951–1980; level or slightly falling 1880–1910 and 1940–1975, rising since; year-to-year (ENSO) variation is serially correlated

label: Life expectancy and income by country, 2007
source: Gapminder (https://www.gapminder.org/data/, CC BY 4.0), via the R package gapminder by Jennifer Bryan (https://github.com/jennybc/gapminder, CC0), retrieved 2026-11-06
note: 142 countries; GDP per capita in inflation-adjusted US dollars, x its base-10 log; life expectancy at birth, years; rises steeply at low incomes and levels off above about $20,000 (4.3), with low outliers mostly in southern Africa (HIV)

label: Montana traffic deaths per 100 million vehicle miles, 1980–2023
source: deaths: NHTSA Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS), national accident files 1980–2023 (https://www.nhtsa.gov/research-data/fatality-analysis-reporting-system-fars, retrieved 2026-11-06), STATE = 30, FATALS summed by year; vehicle miles: FHWA Highway Statistics table VM-2, Montana (1980–1995 from Highway Statistics Summary to 1995, vm202.xlw; 1996–2023 from each year's VM-2, https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/policyinformation/statistics.cfm); US government data, public domain
note: rate: deaths per 100 million vehicle miles on all public roads; rural_interstate_rate: the same on rural interstates, from 20–59 deaths a year, so noisier (crashes coded as rural interstate: 1980 by class of trafficway and land use, 1981 by road function and land use, 1982–2014 road function 1, from 2015 functional system 1 and rural); vmt columns in millions of miles. Rural interstate speed limits: 55 mph until April 1987, then 65 mph; no numeric daytime limit from December 8, 1995 ("reasonable and prudent"); 75 mph from May 1999, after State v. Stanko (December 1998); 80 mph from October 1, 2015. The rate falls from 4.9 in 1980 to about 2.2–2.5 around 1990 and 1.4–1.9 in the 2010s, as nationally; 1997 is high (2.82; 2.73 on rural interstates), and 2020–21 rise, as nationally. FHWA's functional classes changed in 2009 and urban boundaries in 2013 (Montana's urban miles rose by a quarter), which moved some miles from rural to urban roads

label: Montana traffic deaths per month, 1987–2004 (counts), around the end of its daytime speed limit
source: NHTSA Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS), national accident files 1987–2004 (https://www.nhtsa.gov/research-data/fatality-analysis-reporting-system-fars, static.nhtsa.gov/nhtsa/downloads/FARS/, retrieved 2026-11-06), STATE = 30, deaths (FATALS) summed by month; US government data, public domain
note: deaths in crashes on public roads in Montana, at mid-month (decimal year); rural_interstate: crashes on rural interstates (ROAD_FNC = 1), interstate: on interstate routes (ROUTE = 1). Montana had 65 mph on rural interstates from 1987; after the national maximum was repealed, from December 8, 1995 it had no numeric daytime limit on rural highways ("reasonable and prudent"), which the Montana Supreme Court found unconstitutionally vague (State v. Stanko, December 1998); a 75 mph interstate limit followed in May 1999. Yearly deaths 192–215 in 1988–1996, 265 in 1997, 220–269 after. Counts (about 18 a month), with more deaths in summer, so the noise is seasonal and grows with the level; not adjusted for miles driven (montana-traffic-death-rate has yearly rates per mile)

label: Nile annual flow at Aswan, 1871–1970
source: R datasets::Nile; Durbin & Koopman (2001), Time Series Analysis by State Space Methods; Cobb (1978), Biometrika 65:243–251
note: annual flow in 10⁸ m³, "with apparent changepoint near 1898" (Cobb 1978); the example in R's help fits ar(Nile), which selects order 2: the noise is serially correlated

label: Oklahoma earthquakes of magnitude 3 or more per month, 1990–2025
source: USGS ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog (ComCat), events of magnitude ≥ 3 in 33.6–37° N, 94.4–103° W with "Oklahoma" in the place name (https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/, retrieved 2026-11-06); USGS data, public domain
note: count of earthquakes per month at mid-month (decimal year); at most a few a year until 2008, then a surge to 80–116 a month in late 2015 and January 2016, linked to the disposal of wastewater by deep injection, and a decline after injection was cut back in 2016; counts, so the spread grows with the level

label: Song ratings by relative age
source: Davies, Page, Driesener, Anesbury, Yang & Bruwer (2022), The power of nostalgia: Age and preference for popular music, Marketing Letters 33, 681–692, https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11002-022-09626-7; Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License, https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
note: peak around 17 (the paper's two-lines test puts it at 16.8); song age is the listener's age when the song was in the Billboard Top 10 (negative: before birth); rating is each respondent's standardized rating, averaged by song age

label: US coal production data
source: John Tukey's Exploratory Data Analysis book
note: sinusoidal pattern

label: xkcd 2048, Curve-Fitting
source: Randall Munroe, xkcd 2048 (2018-09-19), https://xkcd.com/2048/, CC BY-NC 2.5; points digitized from the comic's 2x image (the same 31 dots in every panel; LINEAR and LINEAR, NO SLOPE agree to 0.3 px)
note: units are comic pixels from the axes' corner (the comic has no scales); two dots share an x; the comic's point is that many curves fit these data
